title: A starburst shines in infrared
caption: The starburst galaxy Messier 82, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
celestial: M82 · constellation Ursa Major · about 12 million light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: Ranked #40 on ESA/Webb’s published “Top 100 Images” list (an institutional selection, not an audience score).

story: A blue-white disc runs from top to bottom through this image, while gas erupts from its bright center forming an hourglass of red and orange dusty clouds on both sides. This is the central part of Messier 82, the Cigar Galaxy, just 12 million light-years away in Ursa Major, seen by Webb's NIRCam.

M82 is a smaller galaxy than ours, yet it shines five times as brightly and forms stars ten times faster. That pace is far quicker than expected for a galaxy of its mass, which is why it is classed as a starburst. In visible light, thick dusty clouds hide the central activity, but Webb's infrared view draws them back. Researchers suspect a gravitational encounter with a larger neighboring spiral sent gas pouring into M82's center millions of years ago, fueling more than 100 super star clusters, each holding hundreds of thousands of stars.
The newborn stars in these clusters blast the surrounding gas with radiation and particles, launching the outflowing wind that Webb traces.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (5.85 x 2.47 arcminutes) and distance (12 million light years), the frame spans roughly 20,000 × 8,600 light-years. Its light set out about 12 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Webb's NIRCam observed in near-infrared light. Blue and cyan show shorter wavelengths including iron emission, green molecular hydrogen, and orange and red PAH emission and the longest filter.
understand.eye: This near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and it passes through dust clouds that hide M82's center in visible light.

behind.people: See full credit: ESA/Webb, NASA & CSA, A. Bolatto
behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.
behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).
behind.processing: Colors assigned by filter, as listed.

explore: Emission from PAH molecules outlines plumes only about 160 light-years wide, made of separate clouds 16–49 light-years across that appear to have been swept off the disc by the winds. An earlier Webb NIRCam image zoomed in on the very core, while this one takes a broader view of the center.
alt: The center of galaxy M82, a blue-white disc running top to bottom with an hourglass-shaped plume of red and orange dust erupting to the left and right, and distant galaxies behind.
